desc:
The digital root of a positive integer is found by repeatedly replacing it with the sum of its decimal digits until a single digit remains. For example, 38 becomes 11 and then 2, so its digital root is 2.

Given lo, hi and a digit d, count the integers x with lo ≤ x ≤ hi whose digital root equals d. Do not loop over the range: it can contain two billion numbers.

lo = 1,  hi = 20, d = 2 -> 3   (2, 11 and 20)
lo = 10, hi = 18, d = 9 -> 1   (only 18)
lo = 1,  hi = 9,  d = 9 -> 1   (only 9)
hints: Count the qualifying numbers in 1..hi and subtract the count in 1..lo-1, so you only need a prefix count.
The digital root of x equals d exactly when x leaves remainder d when divided by 9. A digital root of 9 corresponds to remainder 0.
For a remainder r, the numbers 1..n with x % 9 == r can be counted with integer division. For r = 0 the number 0 must be excluded, because the sequence starts at 1.
editorial: For a positive integer x, the digital root is 1 + (x - 1) % 9, because repeated digit sums preserve the value modulo 9, and the only single digits with a given residue are 1 to 9. So digital root d is the same as x mod 9 = d mod 9.
Let r = d % 9. The count of x in [0, n] with x % 9 == r is (n - r) // 9 + 1 when n ≥ r, else 0. When r = 0, subtract one for x = 0. Define upto(n) this way and the answer is upto(hi) - upto(lo - 1).
The whole query takes constant time, and the intermediate results stay within the range of the answer, which is at most two billion.
